topic: C4.2 Transfers of energy and matter
subject: biology

items.q: Which statement correctly describes an ecosystem as a system?
items.correct: It is an open system: energy enters and leaves it and so does matter, such as water, gases and organisms.
items.misconception: It is a closed system: light energy enters and heat leaves, but all of its matter is recycled within it.
items.why: The phrase 'balance of nature' and diagrams of nutrient cycles drawn as closed loops within one box give the impression of a self-contained unit, and sealed bottle gardens are sometimes used as classroom models of an ecosystem. Ecosystems are open systems in which both energy and matter can enter and exit. Cycles of matter within an ecosystem are never completely closed; water, gases, mineral ions and organisms move across the boundary. Only in a closed system is matter unable to pass in or out.
items.specStatementText: Ecosystems are open: energy and matter both cross the boundary
items.random_wrong: It is a closed system: neither energy nor matter can cross its boundary once the community is established.

items.q: A glass bottle containing soil, moss and small plants was sealed in 1972 and left on a windowsill. The plants are still alive decades later. How should this bottle garden be classified as a system, and why?
items.correct: Closed, because light energy enters through the glass and heat leaves, but no matter passes in or out.
items.misconception: Isolated, because nothing at all crosses the glass, so the plants survive on the energy that was sealed in with them.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'closed' is 'completely shut', so students assume a closed system is sealed against everything, and they have not met the distinction between a closed system and an isolated one. In closed systems only energy is able to pass in and out; matter cannot. A sealed bottle garden is closed to matter but still receives light energy and loses heat, which is why the organisms inside can survive.
items.specStatementText: Ecosystems are open: energy and matter both cross the boundary
items.random_wrong: Closed, because energy is recycled inside the bottle between plants and decomposers, so nothing needs to enter.

items.q: Dense communities of tube worms, clams and shrimps live around hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor, far below the depth to which light penetrates. What is the principal source of the energy that sustains these communities?
items.correct: Bacteria that fix carbon using energy released by oxidizing inorganic substances emerging from the vents.
items.misconception: Dead organic matter produced by photosynthesis at the surface, sinking down to the vents from the sunlit water above.
items.why: Every food chain students construct starts with a green plant, and 'the Sun is the source of all energy' is repeated as a rule from primary school onwards. Sunlight sustains most ecosystems, but there are exceptions. Around deep-sea hydrothermal vents and in some caves, chemoautotrophic bacteria fix carbon using energy released by oxidizing inorganic substances, and these bacteria are the base of the food chains.
items.specStatementText: Sunlight powers almost every ecosystem, and laws describe rather than explain
items.random_wrong: Bacteria that photosynthesize using the faint light emitted by the hot, mineral-rich water leaving the vents.

items.q: A rabbit eats grass and is later eaten by a fox. In what form does chemical energy pass from the rabbit to the fox?
items.correct: In the carbon compounds of the rabbit's tissues, which the fox digests, absorbs and later oxidizes in cell respiration.
items.misconception: In the ATP stored in the rabbit's cells, which the fox absorbs intact and uses directly as its energy currency.
items.why: ATP is introduced as 'the energy currency' and 'the molecule that stores energy', so students expect it to be the molecule that carries energy from prey to predator. Chemical energy passes to a consumer as it feeds on the organism that is the previous stage in the food chain. That energy is held in the carbon compounds of the food; ATP is made inside the consumer's own cells when it oxidizes those compounds in cell respiration.
items.specStatementText: Chemical energy passes along the chain by feeding
items.random_wrong: In the heat of the rabbit's body, which is transferred to the fox and then recycled back to the grass when the fox dies.

items.q: In a local hedgerow, caterpillars and aphids both feed on hawthorn leaves. Blue tits eat caterpillars, ladybirds eat aphids, and sparrowhawks eat blue tits. Which is a correctly constructed food chain from this community?
items.correct: hawthorn leaves → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk
items.misconception: sparrowhawk → blue tit → caterpillar → hawthorn
items.why: Students read an arrow as a verb, 'fox → rabbit' as 'the fox eats the rabbit', and everyday diagrams of who-hunts-whom point at the prey. Arrows in food chains and food webs indicate the direction of transfer of energy and biomass, so they point from the food to the feeder: grass → rabbit → fox.
items.specStatementText: Drawing food chains and webs
items.random_wrong: hawthorn → caterpillar → aphid → ladybird → sparrowhawk

items.q: What do the arrows in a food web represent?
items.correct: The direction in which energy and biomass are transferred, from each organism to the organism that feeds on it.
items.misconception: Every ecological interaction in the community, including competition between species that share a food source.
items.why: Food webs are introduced as diagrams of 'the relationships in a community', so students add links for every relationship they can think of, such as competition or living in the same place. Food chains and food webs represent feeding relationships only. An arrow shows the transfer of energy and biomass from an organism to the organism that consumes it; competitors that share a food source are not joined to each other.
items.specStatementText: Drawing food chains and webs
items.random_wrong: The direction in which each consumer seeks its food, pointing from the feeder to the organism that it eats.

items.q: What is the source of energy for decomposers such as soil fungi and bacteria?
items.correct: Carbon compounds in organic matter from dead organisms, including faeces, dead parts of organisms and dead whole organisms.
items.misconception: Simple inorganic substances in the soil, from which decomposers synthesize their own carbon compounds using energy from sunlight.
items.why: Nutrient cycle diagrams show decomposers releasing minerals that plants take up, and the word 'produce' is heard in that description, so decomposers are placed at the start of the chain. Decomposers obtain their energy as carbon compounds in organic matter coming from dead organisms: faeces, dead parts of organisms and dead whole organisms. They release the elements in that matter, but they do not fix carbon or supply energy to producers.
items.specStatementText: Decomposers live on dead organic matter
items.random_wrong: Dead whole organisms and dead parts of organisms only, because faeces are waste from which all of the energy has been removed.

items.q: A photoautotroph fixes carbon dioxide into carbon compounds and then uses these to build macromolecules such as starch and cellulose. Which statement about the energy involved is correct?
items.correct: Both carbon fixation and the anabolic reactions that build macromolecules need energy, supplied ultimately by light.
items.misconception: The autotroph generates its own energy as it synthesizes the carbon compounds, so no external energy source is needed.
items.why: The phrase 'plants make their own food' is heard as 'plants make their own energy', and food and energy are not separated in everyday speech. Autotrophs use external energy sources to synthesize carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances. Energy is required for carbon fixation and for the anabolic reactions that build macromolecules; it comes from light in photoautotrophs and from oxidation reactions in chemoautotrophs.
items.specStatementText: Autotrophs build carbon compounds from inorganic ones, using outside energy
items.random_wrong: Energy is needed for carbon fixation, but the anabolic reactions run on light directly because photoautotrophs do not respire.

items.q: Iron-oxidizing bacteria live in mine drainage water in darkness. How do they obtain the energy they need to synthesize carbon compounds?
items.correct: From the oxidation of iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions, which releases energy that is used to fix carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: From photosynthesis, using pigments that can capture the very low levels of light reaching the mine drainage water.
items.why: Every producer met before IB is a photosynthesizer, and 'autotroph' is often introduced simply as another word for 'plant'. Autotrophs use external energy sources; light is the source in photoautotrophs and oxidation reactions are the source in chemoautotrophs. Iron-oxidizing bacteria fix carbon using energy from oxidizing iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions, without any light.
items.specStatementText: Light for photoautotrophs, oxidation reactions for chemoautotrophs
items.random_wrong: From cell respiration of carbon compounds that they absorb from the organic matter dissolved in the water.

items.q: A bacterial culture was kept in complete darkness in a medium containing only dissolved iron(II) ions, carbon dioxide, oxygen and mineral salts, with no carbon compounds. Over several days the bacterial biomass increased and iron(III) accumulated. What is the best conclusion?
items.correct: The bacteria are chemoautotrophs that used energy from oxidizing iron(II) to synthesize carbon compounds from carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: The bacteria respired carbon compounds present as contaminants, and the iron(III) formed by ordinary chemical rusting.
items.why: The only oxidation reaction students associate with energy release is the oxidation of glucose in cell respiration, so 'oxidation as an energy source' is assumed to mean respiring organic matter. Oxidation reactions release energy, which makes them useful in living organisms. Chemoautotrophs oxidize inorganic substances, not carbon compounds, and use the energy to synthesize their own carbon compounds from carbon dioxide; that is what makes them autotrophs.
items.specStatementText: Light for photoautotrophs, oxidation reactions for chemoautotrophs
items.random_wrong: The culture must have been exposed to some light, because synthesizing carbon compounds from carbon dioxide requires light.

items.q: A heterotroph eats food containing proteins. Which statement describes how it uses the carbon compounds in this food?
items.correct: It digests the proteins to amino acids, absorbs these and assimilates them by building the specific proteins that it needs.
items.misconception: It absorbs the proteins intact through its gut wall and uses them directly, since a protein from food is already functional.
items.why: Statements such as 'you get protein from meat' suggest that the protein eaten is the protein used, and the need for a heterotroph to make its own specific proteins is not obvious. Heterotrophs use carbon compounds obtained from other organisms to synthesize the carbon compounds that they require. Proteins and nucleic acids are digested externally or internally and are then assimilated by constructing the required compounds from the products.
items.specStatementText: Heterotrophs digest, absorb and rebuild
items.random_wrong: It can use the proteins only if it has a gut, because digestion of complex carbon compounds cannot take place outside a cell.

items.q: A bracket fungus grows on a dead tree trunk. How does it obtain the carbon compounds it requires from the wood?
items.correct: It secretes enzymes onto the wood, absorbs the small molecules produced by this external digestion and assimilates them.
items.misconception: It takes fragments of wood into its cells and digests them internally, since digestion can only happen inside an organism.
items.why: Digestion is taught in the context of the human digestive system, so students equate digestion with the gut and think of fungi as simply 'absorbing' or 'soaking up' their food. Complex carbon compounds are digested either externally or internally. Fungi and saprotrophic bacteria secrete digestive enzymes onto dead organic matter, digest it outside their cells and absorb the products, which are then assimilated.
items.specStatementText: Heterotrophs digest, absorb and rebuild
items.random_wrong: It synthesizes its own carbon compounds from the mineral ions in the decaying wood, using the energy released by decay.

items.q: Which organisms release energy by the oxidation of carbon compounds in cell respiration?
items.correct: All autotrophs and all heterotrophs, in every living cell, throughout the day and the night.
items.misconception: Heterotrophs at all times, but autotrophs only at night, when they cannot obtain energy from photosynthesis.
items.why: Photosynthesis and respiration are presented as opposite equations, which suggests they are alternatives, and the observation that plants release oxygen by day and carbon dioxide at night is read as 'switching' between the two. Energy is released in both autotrophs and heterotrophs by oxidation of carbon compounds in cell respiration. Plants respire continuously; in the light the rate of photosynthesis usually exceeds the rate of respiration, so there is a net uptake of carbon dioxide, but respiration has not stopped.
items.specStatementText: Every organism respires, all the time
items.random_wrong: Only organisms with lungs or gills, because respiration depends on breathing to take in oxygen from the air or water.

items.q: In a garden, blackbirds eat berries from shrubs and also eat snails, which feed on the leaves of the same shrubs. Which trophic level or levels does the blackbird occupy?
items.correct: A primary consumer in the chain where it eats berries and a secondary consumer in the chain where it eats snails.
items.misconception: A secondary consumer only, because each species has a single trophic level that is fixed by its usual diet.
items.why: Textbook food chains show each organism once, in a single position, and classification of animals as herbivores or carnivores suggests a fixed category. Organisms are classified into trophic levels by their position in a particular food chain. An omnivore such as a bear is a primary consumer when eating berries and a secondary consumer when eating a herbivorous fish, so it occupies more than one trophic level.
items.specStatementText: Trophic levels are positions, not types of feeder
items.random_wrong: Secondary consumer in both chains, because a bird that eats animals is a carnivore and carnivores are secondary consumers.

items.q: In a classic study of the Silver Springs ecosystem in Florida, the energy flow through each trophic level (all in kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹) was: producers 20 810; primary consumers 3368; secondary consumers 383; tertiary consumers 21. What percentage of the energy at the primary consumer level was transferred to the secondary consumers?
items.correct: About 11%
items.misconception: About 1.8%
items.why: Energy pyramids present the producer bar as the obvious baseline, and students used to 'percentage change' calculations reach for a subtraction. Energy pyramids show energy transfer and energy losses between successive trophic levels, so the percentage transferred at each step is the ratio of the energy at that level to the energy at the level immediately below, expressed as a percentage.
items.specStatementText: Energy pyramids show flow, not stock
items.random_wrong: Exactly 10%

items.q: Why is much less energy available to the secondary consumers in a food chain than to the primary consumers?
items.correct: Not all primary consumers are eaten, not all of what is eaten is absorbed, and most absorbed energy is released as heat in respiration.
items.misconception: Primary consumers use up most of their energy in moving and feeding, so that energy is destroyed and no longer exists.
items.why: Everyday phrases such as 'using up energy' and 'running out of energy' suggest energy can be consumed, and the eventual conversion to heat is not visible. Energy is not destroyed. Energy that is not passed on to the next trophic level is converted to heat in cell respiration, either by the organism or by the decomposers and detritus feeders that respire its dead parts and faeces, and leaves the ecosystem as heat.
items.specStatementText: Most energy is lost at each step
items.random_wrong: Decomposers, which form the final trophic level, take the energy from primary consumers and return it to the producers.

items.q: A caterpillar ingests leaf material containing 100 kJ of energy. It egests 50 kJ in faeces, releases 35 kJ as heat through cell respiration and stores 15 kJ in new biomass. What happens to the energy in the faeces?
items.correct: It passes to decomposers and detritus feeders, which release it as heat in respiration, not to the next trophic level.
items.misconception: It is returned to the plant through the soil, so that the plant can use it again for growth instead of needing sunlight.
items.why: Energy flow and nutrient cycling are taught together, and diagrams that show decomposers returning material to plants are read as if they show energy being returned as well. An ecosystem needs a continuous input of energy because every transfer releases heat that cannot be reused. Decomposers return the elements in dead matter to the abiotic environment, but the chemical energy in that matter is released as heat, not passed back to producers.
items.specStatementText: Most energy is lost at each step
items.random_wrong: There is no usable energy in the faeces, because the 50 kJ was already released as heat inside the caterpillar's gut.

items.q: Why do plants, as well as animals, lose heat to their environment?
items.correct: Cell respiration in every organism converts some chemical energy to heat, both when ATP is produced and when ATP is used.
items.misconception: They do not: heat is produced only by warm-blooded animals; plants merely lose heat that they absorbed from sunlight.
items.why: Body heat is noticed in mammals and birds, and plants and insects feel cold, so heat production is linked to being 'warm-blooded' rather than to respiration. Heat loss to the environment occurs in both autotrophs and heterotrophs due to conversion of chemical energy to heat in cell respiration. Every organism that respires produces heat; endotherms differ only in generating enough, and retaining enough, to keep a high body temperature.
items.specStatementText: All organisms leak heat, making and using ATP
items.random_wrong: Plants respire only at night, so the heat they lose is produced in darkness and simply builds up until the next day.

items.q: Food chains in most ecosystems have no more than four or five trophic levels. What is the reason for this restriction?
items.correct: So much energy is lost at each transfer that after a few levels too little remains to support a viable consumer population.
items.misconception: The number of trophic levels is set by the number of species in the community, and few communities have more than five.
items.why: Food web diagrams for richer communities look more complicated, and students count links rather than thinking about the energy available at each level. Restrictions on the number of trophic levels are due to energy losses. A large proportion of the energy at each level is lost as heat or passes to decomposers, so the energy remaining after a few transfers cannot sustain another population of consumers, however many species are present.
items.specStatementText: Energy losses cap food chains at four or five levels
items.random_wrong: The tissues of organisms higher in the chain contain less energy per gram, so a predator cannot gain enough energy from each meal.

items.q: In a model grassland ecosystem the dry biomass per square metre is: producers 800 g, primary consumers 100 g, secondary consumers 15 g, tertiary consumers 2 g. Samples of dry biomass from each level release similar amounts of energy per gram when burned. Which conclusion is supported?
items.correct: Energy per unit mass is similar at every level, so the fall in energy available up the chain is due to the fall in biomass.
items.misconception: The data show that producers accumulate 800 g of biomass per square metre each year, which is their primary production.
items.why: Both quantities are measured by harvesting and drying vegetation, and a large forest obviously has a large biomass, so the stock and the rate are conflated. Primary production is the accumulation of carbon compounds in biomass by autotrophs. Its units are mass of carbon per unit area per unit time, usually g m⁻² yr⁻¹. Biomass accumulates when organisms grow or reproduce; the biomass present is the result of production over time, minus losses.
items.specStatementText: Energy losses cap food chains at four or five levels
items.random_wrong: The biomass at higher levels must be poorer in energy per gram, since energy falls even faster than mass along the chain.

items.q: Which are the correct units for primary production?
items.correct: Grams of carbon per square metre per year
items.misconception: Kilojoules per square metre per year
items.why: Pyramids of numbers and pyramids of biomass, met before IB, are snapshots of what is present, so students assume an energy pyramid is a snapshot too. Energy pyramids represent energy transfer and energy losses between trophic levels, using research data from specific ecosystems. Each bar is a rate of energy flow, which is why the units include per unit time.
items.specStatementText: Primary production is a rate of carbon accumulation
items.random_wrong: Grams of carbon per square metre of land

items.q: A widely cited compilation of net primary production (g of dry biomass m⁻² yr⁻¹) gives typical values of about 2200 for tropical rainforest, 600 for temperate grassland, 125 for open ocean and 90 for desert. What do these data show?
items.correct: Biomes differ greatly in capacity to accumulate biomass; deserts have high light but water limits their photosynthesis.
items.misconception: The desert value must be an error, because deserts receive the most sunlight and primary production depends on light alone.
items.why: Light is the energy source for photosynthesis and is emphasized as the factor that drives it, so other limiting factors such as water and temperature are overlooked. Biomes vary in their capacity to accumulate biomass. Photosynthesis needs water and suitable temperatures as well as light, and mineral nutrients are needed for growth, so primary production is highest where all of these are available and very low in deserts and polar regions.
items.specStatementText: Primary production is a rate of carbon accumulation
items.random_wrong: Rainforest has the highest value simply because it contains the most standing biomass, not because it grows faster.

items.q: In every ecosystem, secondary production is lower than primary production. What is the reason for this?
items.correct: Heterotrophs convert much of the carbon they consume to carbon dioxide and water in cell respiration, so less becomes biomass.
items.misconception: Everything a heterotroph absorbs becomes biomass, so secondary production is lower only because heterotrophs eat relatively little.
items.why: 'You are what you eat' and the assimilation step in digestion suggest that absorbed food becomes body tissue, while the loss of carbon as exhaled carbon dioxide is invisible. Secondary production is lower than primary production because heterotrophs lose biomass when carbon compounds are converted to carbon dioxide and water in cell respiration. Only the carbon compounds that are not respired can accumulate as growth or reproduction.
items.specStatementText: Secondary production is lower than primary
items.random_wrong: The biomass of heterotrophs contains less energy per gram than plant biomass, so less carbon is stored in each gram.

items.q: A student draws a carbon cycle diagram for a pond. Which set of labelled arrows is correct?
items.correct: Photosynthesis: CO₂ → producers; feeding: producers → consumers; respiration: producers, consumers, decomposers → CO₂.
items.misconception: Photosynthesis: CO₂ → producers; feeding: producers → consumers; decomposition of dead organisms → CO₂, with no other return.
items.why: Carbon cycle diagrams give prominence to the 'death and decay' arrow, and respiration by living organisms is drawn as a small side arrow or omitted. In a carbon cycle diagram, respiration by producers, consumers and decomposers all return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. A living organism releases carbon dioxide every day of its life; decomposition is the route for the carbon that remains in dead organic matter.
items.specStatementText: Drawing the carbon cycle
items.random_wrong: Absorption: soil carbon → producers; feeding: producers → consumers; respiration: all organisms → CO₂ in the air and water.

items.q: Suppose measurements in a forest over one year give: carbon fixed by photosynthesis 1200 g m⁻²; carbon released by plant respiration 600 g m⁻²; carbon released by the respiration of animals, fungi and bacteria 650 g m⁻². Is the forest a carbon sink or a carbon source in that year?
items.correct: A carbon source, with a net release of 50 g m⁻², because total respiration (1250) exceeds photosynthesis (1200).
items.misconception: A carbon sink, because a forest full of photosynthesizing trees removes carbon dioxide no matter what its respiration is.
items.why: Trees are described as 'absorbing' or 'soaking up' carbon dioxide, and the respiration of the plants themselves and of decomposers in the soil is not considered. If photosynthesis exceeds respiration there is a net uptake of carbon dioxide and the ecosystem is a sink; if respiration exceeds photosynthesis there is a net release and it is a source. Respiration here includes all organisms, including the plants and the decomposers.
items.specStatementText: Sink or source depends on photosynthesis versus respiration
items.random_wrong: A carbon sink, with a net uptake of 550 g m⁻², because only heterotroph respiration returns carbon to the atmosphere.

items.q: Which statement about the combustion of biomass, peat, coal, oil and natural gas is correct?
items.correct: All release carbon dioxide that was originally fixed by photosynthesis, at dates ranging from recent years to hundreds of millions of years ago.
items.misconception: All formed from organisms at about the same time in the distant past, so burning any of them has the same significance for the carbon cycle.
items.why: 'Fossil fuels' are taught as one category with one story, that they formed from ancient organisms under pressure. Combustion of biomass, peat, coal, oil and natural gas all release carbon dioxide, but these carbon sinks vary in date of formation, from recent biomass, through peat that has accumulated over thousands of years, to coal, oil and gas that are millions of years old.
items.specStatementText: Burning returns fixed carbon to the air
items.random_wrong: Burning biomass such as wood releases no carbon dioxide because it is renewable, whereas burning the fossil fuels does release it.

items.q: Three events release carbon dioxide: a lightning strike ignites a dry grassland; a farmer burns crop stubble after harvest; a power station burns coal. Which comparison is correct?
items.correct: All three are combustion releasing carbon dioxide; the first is natural, but human activity has greatly increased combustion rates.
items.misconception: Only the coal releases carbon dioxide, because the grass and the stubble are renewable biomass and so are carbon-neutral fuels.
items.why: 'Carbon-neutral' and 'renewable' are heard as 'produces no carbon dioxide', when they refer to the balance over time between combustion and regrowth. Release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere occurs during combustion of biomass as well as of peat, coal, oil and natural gas. The difference is only in how recently the carbon was fixed and whether it is likely to be fixed again.
items.specStatementText: Burning returns fixed carbon to the air
items.random_wrong: The carbon in the coal and the carbon in the stubble were both fixed at about the same time, so the three releases are all equivalent.

items.q: At Mauna Loa, atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration rises to a peak each May and falls to a minimum each September or October, a swing of several parts per million. What causes this annual fluctuation?
items.correct: In the Northern Hemisphere growing season photosynthesis exceeds respiration, drawing carbon dioxide down; in autumn and winter respiration exceeds photosynthesis.
items.misconception: People burn more fuel for heating in the Northern Hemisphere winter, so combustion raises carbon dioxide until spring and it falls again in summer.
items.why: Students know combustion of fossil fuels raises carbon dioxide and that heating is seasonal, so they apply the same cause to both the trend and the fluctuation. The annual fluctuation is analysed in terms of photosynthesis and respiration: the seasonal growth of vegetation, mostly in the Northern Hemisphere where most land lies, draws carbon dioxide down from May to September, after which respiration and decomposition dominate. The long-term rising trend is the part that combustion explains.
items.specStatementText: Reading the Keeling Curve
items.random_wrong: Plants respire only in winter, when they cannot photosynthesize, so carbon dioxide is released only in the cold months and absorbed in the warm months.

items.q: The annual mean carbon dioxide concentration at Mauna Loa was about 317 ppm in 1960 and about 414 ppm in 2020. What is the accepted explanation for this long-term trend?
items.correct: Combustion of fossil fuels and biomass releases carbon fixed long ago faster than photosynthesis and other processes remove it.
items.misconception: Breathing by the growing human population, together with its livestock, has added more carbon dioxide each year than plants can absorb.
items.why: Students learn that respiration produces carbon dioxide and that the human population is growing, and combine the two. The long-term trend is analysed in terms of combustion: burning fossil fuels adds to the atmosphere carbon that was removed from it by photosynthesis millions of years ago. Respiration returns carbon fixed within recent years and does not change the total in circulation.
items.specStatementText: Reading the Keeling Curve
items.random_wrong: Increased volcanic activity has released carbon dioxide from deep within the Earth, and this geological source dominates the trend.

items.q: Which statement about the recycling of chemical elements in ecosystems is correct?
items.correct: All elements required by organisms are recycled; decomposers release them from dead matter in forms that autotrophs can take up.
items.misconception: Only carbon is recycled; the other elements are absorbed from the soil, used by organisms and then used up, so they must be replaced.
items.why: The carbon cycle is the only nutrient cycle studied in detail, and fertilizer use suggests that soil minerals are consumed and must be replaced from outside. All elements used by living organisms, not just carbon, are recycled in ecosystems. Elements are not destroyed when organisms use them; they are returned to the abiotic environment, with decomposers playing a key role.
items.specStatementText: Every element is recycled, and decomposers make it happen
items.random_wrong: Elements are released from dead organisms automatically as they die, so decomposers play only a minor part in recycling them.

items.q: A farmer harvests and sells the whole crop from a field every year and returns no plant material or manure. Soil analysis shows that the mineral nutrients available to plants decline year on year. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The elements built into crop biomass are removed from the field instead of being returned by decomposers, so the cycle is broken.
items.misconception: The crop absorbed carbon compounds from the soil to build up its biomass, and it is this carbon that the soil is running short of.
items.why: Plants are 'fed' with fertilizer, roots visibly take things up from soil, and the idea that a tree's mass came almost entirely from a gas is counter-intuitive. Autotrophs synthesize carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances: carbon dioxide is fixed using an external energy source. The carbon in plant biomass comes from atmospheric carbon dioxide, which is why photosynthesis is the route by which carbon enters ecosystems.
items.specStatementText: Every element is recycled, and decomposers make it happen
items.random_wrong: Mineral elements are used up and destroyed by the growing plants, so any field loses them whether or not the crop is removed.

items.q: In the Silver Springs study the energy flow through the trophic levels (kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹) was: producers 20 810; primary consumers 3368; secondary consumers 383; tertiary consumers 21. Which statement about an energy pyramid constructed from these data is correct?
items.correct: Four horizontal bars with producers at the base, each bar's width proportional to the energy flowing through that level per unit area per unit time.
items.misconception: The bars represent the energy stored in the organisms present at each level when sampled, so the units should be kcal m⁻² with no time component.
items.why: Pyramids of numbers and pyramids of biomass, met before IB, are snapshots of what is present, so students assume an energy pyramid is a snapshot too. Energy pyramids represent energy transfer and energy losses between trophic levels, using research data from specific ecosystems. Each bar is a rate of energy flow, which is why the units include per unit time.
items.specStatementText: Energy pyramids show flow, not stock
items.random_wrong: A fifth bar for decomposers should be drawn at the top, because they form the final trophic level and receive the remaining 21 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.

items.q: Would a single ecosystem that does not fit a generalization such as the 10% rule show that the generalization is useless?
items.correct: No. A useful generalization describes the pattern in the great majority of cases and allows predictions; it is a rule of thumb, so known exceptions do not make it useless.
items.misconception: A scientific law holds without any exception, so an ecosystem that does not fit a law such as the 10% rule proves the law false.
items.why: The word 'law' suggests a rule that must be obeyed, and students are taught in other contexts that one contradictory observation falsifies a hypothesis. Laws in science are generalized principles or rules of thumb. Useful generalizations summarize many observations, hold in most cases and make testable predictions; a rule of thumb such as 'about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level' is useful even though real transfers range widely around that value.
items.specStatementText: Sunlight powers almost every ecosystem, and laws describe rather than explain
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do faeces contain energy that decomposers can use?
items.correct: Yes. Faeces contain undigested carbon compounds whose chemical energy was never absorbed by the animal, so they are an energy source for decomposers and detritus feeders.
items.misconception: Faeces are waste from which the animal has already extracted all the energy, so they cannot supply energy to anything.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'waste' is something used up and worthless, and students assume digestion is complete. Only part of the food an animal eats is digested and absorbed. The rest is egested as faeces, which still contain carbon compounds. Faeces, dead parts of organisms and dead whole organisms all supply energy to decomposers.
items.specStatementText: Decomposers live on dead organic matter
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is cell respiration?
items.correct: The oxidation of carbon compounds inside cells to release energy, used to make ATP. It is a chemical process in every living cell, not the movement of air.
items.misconception: Respiration is breathing, so the organisms that respire are those with lungs or gills, and energy comes from the oxygen breathed in.
items.why: In everyday and medical language 'respiration' means breathing, and gas exchange is the visible part of the process. Cell respiration is the release of energy by oxidation of carbon compounds, and it occurs in all organisms, autotrophs and heterotrophs, including bacteria, fungi and plants that have no breathing organs. Oxygen is used in aerobic respiration, but the energy comes from the carbon compounds, not from the oxygen.
items.specStatementText: Every organism respires, all the time
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every carnivore a secondary consumer?
items.correct: No. A carnivore that feeds on a secondary consumer is a tertiary consumer. Trophic level depends on the position in the food chain, not on the type of food.
items.misconception: The trophic level terms describe kinds of feeder: all herbivores are primary consumers and all carnivores are secondary consumers.
items.why: Students first meet three-organism food chains in which the only carnivore is always the secondary consumer, so 'carnivore' and 'secondary consumer' become synonyms. Producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer and tertiary consumer name successive positions in a food chain. A carnivore eating a herbivore is a secondary consumer; a carnivore eating that carnivore is a tertiary consumer.
items.specStatementText: Trophic levels are positions, not types of feeder
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is exactly 10% of the energy transferred between every pair of trophic levels?
items.correct: No. About 10% is a rule of thumb; measured transfers in real ecosystems vary widely, and the value must be calculated from the data given.
items.misconception: Exactly 10% of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next, in every ecosystem and at every level.
items.why: The '10% rule' is taught as a memorable figure and used in calculations, so it is treated as a fixed law rather than a rough generalization. Reductions in energy availability at each successive stage are due to large energy losses, and the proportion that passes on varies between ecosystems and between levels. Percentage transfer is calculated as energy at the higher level divided by energy at the level below, multiplied by 100.
items.specStatementText: Most energy is lost at each step
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is all the energy released in cell respiration captured in ATP?
items.correct: No. Energy transfers are not 100% efficient, so heat is produced both when ATP is made in cell respiration and again when ATP is used in cells.
items.misconception: Cell respiration transfers all the energy from carbon compounds into ATP, and heat is only released later when ATP is used.
items.why: Respiration is summarized as 'glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP', with no heat in the equation, so students assume the capture in ATP is complete. Energy transfers are not 100% efficient. Some of the energy released by oxidizing carbon compounds becomes heat during ATP production, and when ATP is used to do work in the cell more of the energy becomes heat. Both stages contribute to heat loss to the environment.
items.specStatementText: All organisms leak heat, making and using ATP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the annual fluctuations in atmospheric carbon dioxide large enough to be caused by photosynthesis and respiration?
items.correct: Yes. The fluxes of carbon dioxide between organisms and the atmosphere each year are huge, so the seasonal imbalance between photosynthesis and respiration in the Northern Hemisphere produces a measurable annual cycle of several parts per million.
items.misconception: Biological processes are too small to affect the whole atmosphere, so the annual fluctuation in the Keeling Curve must be due to human activity or to measurement error.
items.why: Photosynthesis is studied at the scale of a leaf or a pondweed experiment, and students have no sense of the global scale of the fluxes. The annual fluctuation is explained by photosynthesis and respiration. The fluxes involved per year are huge; the exchange of carbon dioxide and oxygen between autotrophs and heterotrophs is a major interaction on a global scale.
items.specStatementText: Reading the Keeling Curve
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are decomposers needed for elements to be recycled?
items.correct: Yes. Decomposers break down the carbon compounds in dead organic matter and release the elements in inorganic forms that autotrophs can absorb; without them, elements would remain locked in dead matter.
items.misconception: Elements are released from dead organisms automatically when they die, so decomposers make little difference to recycling.
items.why: Death and decay are seen as one event, and the organisms that carry out decay are invisible, so the chemical work they do is not appreciated. Decomposers play a key role in the recycling of chemical elements. The elements in dead organisms and faeces are combined in complex carbon compounds; decomposers digest these and release the elements as simple inorganic substances that can be taken up again by autotrophs.
items.specStatementText: Every element is recycled, and decomposers make it happen
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a herbivore the first or the second consumer level in a food chain?
items.correct: The first. The producer is not a consumer; a herbivore feeding on the producer is the primary consumer, and the animal that eats it is the secondary consumer.
items.misconception: Producers are the first consumers because they consume sunlight and carbon dioxide, so herbivores are secondary consumers and their predators are tertiary consumers.
items.why: 'Consume' is used loosely for anything an organism takes in, and students count every organism in a chain, including the producer, when assigning 'first', 'second' and 'third'. Use the terms producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer and tertiary consumer. Producers are autotrophs and are not consumers; the numbering of consumers starts with the organism that feeds on the producer.
items.specStatementText: Trophic levels are positions, not types of feeder
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is primary production measured per plant?
items.correct: No. It is measured per unit area of the ecosystem per unit time, usually g m⁻² yr⁻¹, so that ecosystems and biomes can be compared.
items.misconception: Primary production is the growth of an individual plant, so it is measured in grams per plant per year.
items.why: Growth is measured on single plants in practical work, and the idea of a rate for a whole area of ground is not met until ecology. The units of primary production should be mass of carbon per unit area per unit time, usually g m⁻² yr⁻¹. Production is a property of an area of ecosystem, not of a single organism.
items.specStatementText: Primary production is a rate of carbon accumulation
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Did the carbon in coal, oil and natural gas ever pass through living organisms?
items.correct: Yes. Fossil fuels formed from the remains of organisms that were not fully decomposed, so their carbon was originally fixed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis.
items.misconception: Fossil fuels are minerals dug from rocks, so their carbon is of geological origin and has never been part of the carbon cycle.
items.why: Coal and oil are extracted by mining and drilling alongside metal ores, and 'fossil' is not connected to its meaning of preserved remains of organisms. Peat, coal, oil and natural gas are carbon sinks formed from organic matter, and they vary in date of formation. Combustion returns to the atmosphere carbon that photosynthesis removed from it long ago, which is why it raises the atmospheric concentration.
items.specStatementText: Burning returns fixed carbon to the air
